title: General Paper
tagline: The capstone: bring the whole degree together and practise thinking like a biochemist under exam conditions.
overview: BC 4003 is a capstone, integration course. Instead of introducing a new area, it asks you to connect what you have learned across the degree (molecules, enzymes, metabolism, genes, signalling, techniques and the ethics of the field) and to answer unfamiliar, cross-disciplinary questions in clear, exam-style prose. Because the questions are synthetic by design, these units are organised around themes that bridge courses: information flow, structure and function, energy and metabolism, whole-body integration, regulation and signalling, disease mechanisms, techniques and data interpretation, and critical evaluation.
whyItMatters: Real problems, from a patient with unexplained hyperglycaemia to a failed experiment, never arrive labelled with a course code. Being able to bring enzymes, metabolism, genetics and statistics to bear on one question is what turns a graduate from someone who has studied biochemistry into someone who can work as a biochemist.
studyTips: Make one-page concept maps of each theme, linking courses, and redraw them from memory.
Practise answering a question in 20 minutes with a plan, a diagram and one example from each relevant area.
Use past papers, then rewrite weak answers using a model answer or a friend's feedback.
Study with classmates: explain a pathway or technique to each other and ask 'why does the cell do it this way?'
Revise from a general textbook so that you see how topics connect, then check detail in lecture notes.

units.title: Thinking and Writing Across the Degree: Exam Technique for Integrative Questions
units.hook: A General Paper question rarely announces which course it belongs to. 'Why does a drug that blocks a kinase lower blood glucose?' touches enzymes, signalling, metabolism and perhaps pharmacology all at once. The skill being tested is not recall of one lecture but the ability to connect them.
learningObjectives: Read an integrative question and identify the concepts and courses it draws on
Plan an answer with a short outline before writing
Link levels of explanation: molecule, pathway, cell, tissue, organism
Use diagrams and numbers to support a written answer
Allocate time across questions and avoid over-writing a favourite one
Review and improve your answers using a marking-style checklist

keyConcepts.definition: Words such as 'explain', 'compare', 'evaluate' and 'discuss' tell you what kind of answer is required; 'describe' is not the same as 'explain'.
Connecting ideas from different topics into a single coherent explanation.
Answering at molecular, cellular, tissue and whole-organism scales and showing how they relate.
A few lines of bullet points written before the answer to organise structure and avoid omissions.
Using specific examples, experiments, numbers and named molecules rather than generalities.
Distinguishing what is established from what is hypothesised or disputed.

deeper.beginner: Underline the command word and the key nouns in the question. In two minutes, write the main points you want to make and the order in which they connect. Start with a clear direct answer, then support it with mechanism and an example. Draw a small pathway if it helps; label it.
deeper.intermediate: Practise by taking a mechanism (for example insulin signalling) and writing how it would appear in questions from different courses: structure of the receptor, kinases, glucose transport, gene expression, diabetes. Build a one-page concept map for each major theme. Time yourself and mark answers against the question: did you answer what was asked?
deeper.advanced: Learn to move between scales and to reason with unfamiliar data: when a question presents a new situation, use first principles (thermodynamics, kinetics, regulation, information flow) rather than searching for the memorised answer. Be explicit about assumptions and show how alternative explanations could be distinguished by a decisive experiment.

commonMistakes: Writing everything you know about a keyword rather than answering the question
Describing a pathway when the question asks to explain a regulatory logic
Spending most of the time on the first question
Leaving out units, direction of change or the cell/tissue in which something occurs

units.title: Information Flow: From Gene to Protein to Phenotype
units.hook: A single base change in one gene can alter a protein, which changes an enzyme, which changes a pathway, which changes how a child tolerates milk. Following information from DNA to organism is the thread that holds molecular biology together.
learningObjectives: Explain replication, transcription and translation and their key enzymes and signals
Describe how the genetic code and mutations determine protein sequence
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic gene expression and processing
Predict the effect of a mutation at DNA, RNA and protein level
State what the central dogma does and does not say
Link gene expression to cell phenotype and disease

keyConcepts.definition: Sequence information is transferred from nucleic acids to proteins; it is not transferred from protein back to nucleic acid or to another protein.
Synthesis of RNA from a DNA template by RNA polymerase, regulated by promoters and transcription factors.
Synthesis of a protein on a ribosome, reading mRNA codons with tRNA adaptors.
A triplet code that is nearly universal and degenerate: most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon.
A missense mutation changes one amino acid, a nonsense mutation creates a stop codon and a frameshift (insertion or deletion not in multiples of three) alters the reading frame downstream.
In eukaryotes pre-mRNA is capped, spliced and polyadenylated before export.
Copying RNA into DNA, as in retroviruses; consistent with the central dogma as stated by Crick.
Chemical changes to proteins after synthesis, such as phosphorylation or glycosylation, that alter activity or location.

deeper.beginner: DNA is copied to make more DNA, transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein. Mutations alter the DNA, which may alter the RNA and protein. Not all changes matter: the code is degenerate, so some changes are silent. Ask three things of any mutation: where is it, what does it change, and what does the protein do?
deeper.intermediate: Compare prokaryotes (coupled transcription and translation, operons) with eukaryotes (nucleus, splicing, capping, polyadenylation, chromatin). Use a mutation as a worked example: write the DNA, mRNA and protein sequences before and after, and decide whether the change is silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift. Link to function: a missense change in an active site can abolish activity, whereas one on the surface may be tolerated.
deeper.advanced: Integrate regulation at each step: chromatin state, transcription factors and enhancers, RNA stability, microRNAs, alternative splicing, translational control and protein degradation. Recognise that the central dogma limits the direction of sequence information, not the existence of regulation or of RNA-to-DNA transfer by reverse transcriptase. In an exam, show how one defect propagates: for example a splice-site mutation altering exon inclusion, producing a truncated protein that is degraded, with consequences for a pathway.

commonMistakes: Stating that the central dogma says information only flows DNA to RNA to protein, with no exceptions
Forgetting that the genetic code is read in triplets from a start codon
Assuming every mutation changes the protein
Mixing up template and coding strands

selfCheck.question: Which statement about the central dogma is accurate?
options: Information can never flow from RNA to DNA
Sequence information cannot pass from protein back to nucleic acid
DNA is translated directly to protein
selfCheck.explanation: Crick's formulation forbids transfer from protein back to nucleic acid; RNA to DNA by reverse transcriptase is allowed.

selfCheck.question: A single-base deletion in the middle of a coding sequence most likely causes:
options: A frameshift altering all downstream amino acids
A change in only one amino acid
selfCheck.explanation: Removing one base shifts the triplet reading frame for the rest of the message, usually producing a nonfunctional protein.

selfCheck.question: Why can a base substitution be silent?
selfCheck.explanation: Several codons can encode the same amino acid, so some substitutions leave the protein unchanged.

units.title: Proteins and Enzymes: Structure, Folding and Kinetics
units.hook: An enzyme is a shape that happens to make a reaction one hundred million times faster. Understanding why requires putting together amino-acid chemistry, folding, binding energy and the equations that describe rate.
learningObjectives: Relate amino-acid properties to secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure
Explain how sequence determines fold and why proteins misfold
Interpret Michaelis-Menten parameters Vmax and Km and Lineweaver-Burk plots
Distinguish competitive, uncompetitive and non-competitive inhibition
Describe allosteric regulation and covalent modification of enzymes
Use enzyme data to infer mechanisms or the effect of a mutation

keyConcepts.definition: Amino-acid sequence; local folds such as helices and sheets; the overall 3D fold; assembly of several chains.
For many small proteins the amino-acid sequence contains the information for the native fold under suitable conditions.
The region where substrate binds and the reaction is catalysed, formed by residues that may be distant in sequence.
v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) describes the rate as a function of substrate concentration for many single-substrate enzymes.
Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax (an apparent measure of affinity under defined conditions); Vmax is the rate when the enzyme is saturated.
Inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site: apparent Km increases while Vmax is unchanged.
Binding at one site changes activity at another, often producing a sigmoidal rate curve.
A protein that helps others fold and prevents aggregation.

deeper.beginner: Proteins fold because of the properties of their side chains: hydrophobic residues bury, charged ones face water, and many weak interactions add up. An enzyme speeds a reaction by binding the transition state well. Plot rate against substrate: at low substrate it rises steeply, then levels at Vmax.
deeper.intermediate: Practise reading kinetic data. A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but does not change Vmax because excess substrate can outcompete it; a non-competitive inhibitor lowers Vmax. Use a Lineweaver-Burk plot to visualise but fit the data with nonlinear regression. Connect structure to function: a mutation in the active site changes Km or kcat, while one in the core may destabilise the fold.
deeper.advanced: Link thermodynamics and kinetics: catalysts lower activation energy and do not change equilibrium. Consider kcat/Km as a measure of catalytic efficiency, the effect of pH and temperature, and the role of cooperativity and feedback inhibition in controlling metabolic flux. Understand how misfolding and aggregation underlie diseases, and how folding stability is tuned by chaperones and quality control.

commonMistakes: Saying an enzyme 'uses up' during catalysis
Interpreting Km as binding constant without conditions
Mixing up what competitive and non-competitive inhibitors do to Km and Vmax
Forgetting that enzymes do not alter equilibrium

options: Lowering Vmax with no change in Km
Raising apparent Km with no change in Vmax
selfCheck.explanation: Because it competes with substrate, enough substrate can still reach Vmax, but a higher substrate concentration is needed to reach half of it.

units.title: Bioenergetics and Core Metabolism
units.hook: Cells run on a trick: couple an unfavourable reaction to a favourable one, and move electrons downhill to pump protons uphill. Once you see that logic, glycolysis, the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation stop being a list and become one machine.
learningObjectives: Explain how ATP hydrolysis and coupling drive unfavourable reactions
Trace the fate of glucose through glycolysis, the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
Account for ATP yield and the regulation of key steps
Explain chemiosmosis and how uncouplers and inhibitors act
Compare aerobic and anaerobic routes and fermentation
Place fatty acid and amino acid catabolism into the same framework

keyConcepts.definition: A reaction proceeds if the overall delta G is negative; coupling links a favourable reaction to an unfavourable one.
ATP hydrolysis is used to drive many reactions, but the free energy depends on cellular concentrations, not only the standard value.
Conversion of glucose to pyruvate in the cytosol, with net ATP and NADH production, regulated at hexokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase.
Oxidises acetyl-CoA to CO2 in the mitochondrial matrix, generating NADH, FADH2 and GTP/ATP.
Electrons move through membrane complexes to oxygen, pumping protons across the inner membrane.
ATP synthase uses the proton-motive force created by electron transport to make ATP.
A compound that dissipates the proton gradient so that respiration continues but less ATP is made, releasing heat.
Regenerates NAD+ in the absence of oxygen so that glycolysis can continue.

deeper.beginner: Glucose is oxidised stepwise. Glycolysis makes a little ATP and carries electrons on NADH; the TCA cycle strips more electrons; the electron transport chain uses them to pump protons; ATP synthase lets protons flow back and makes ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor.
deeper.intermediate: Connect regulation to need: high ATP and citrate inhibit phosphofructokinase-1, AMP activates it. Use the proton-motive force to explain why cyanide (blocks complex IV) and oligomycin (blocks ATP synthase) both stop respiration but by different mechanisms, and why an uncoupler increases oxygen consumption. Estimate ATP yield but know that the numbers are approximate, depending on the shuttle systems and the proton to ATP ratio.
deeper.advanced: Place energetics in context: standard and actual free energy, the role of mitochondrial transporters and shuttles, tissue differences, and the importance of reactive oxygen species. Consider how regulation by energy charge, redox state and substrate supply integrates catabolism with biosynthesis. Link to disease: mitochondrial disorders, ischaemia and the Warburg effect in tumours.

commonMistakes: Quoting a single 'textbook' ATP number as exact
Saying oxygen is used in the TCA cycle directly
Confusing substrate-level phosphorylation with oxidative phosphorylation
Thinking uncouplers stop electron transport

units.title: Whole-Body Metabolic Integration and Diabetes
units.hook: Between meals your liver quietly keeps your brain supplied with glucose, then after meals it stores the surplus. Insulin and glucagon coordinate organs that never touch each other. When that coordination fails, the result is diabetes: an integration problem as much as a single-enzyme problem.
learningObjectives: Compare metabolism in the fed, fasting and prolonged-fasting states
Explain the roles of liver, muscle, adipose tissue and brain in fuel metabolism
Describe insulin and glucagon signalling and their effects on key enzymes
Explain gluconeogenesis, glycogen metabolism, lipolysis and ketogenesis in context
Explain how insulin resistance and insulin deficiency lead to hyperglycaemia
Predict metabolic consequences of a hormone, enzyme or transporter defect

keyConcepts.definition: After a meal, insulin rises, promoting glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis.
Glucagon and low insulin promote liver glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenesis and release of fatty acids from adipose tissue.
Synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate, amino acids and glycerol, mainly in the liver.
Fatty-acid-derived fuels made by the liver during prolonged fasting that the brain and other tissues can use.
Pathways that return carbon from muscle lactate or alanine to the liver for glucose synthesis.
Insulin binds a receptor tyrosine kinase, activating pathways such as PI3K-Akt that promote GLUT4 translocation in muscle and fat and alter enzyme activity.
Reduced response of tissues to insulin, requiring more hormone to achieve the same effect.
Hormones act through phosphorylation and gene expression to switch key enzymes on or off.

deeper.beginner: After eating, blood glucose rises and insulin tells the liver, muscle and fat to store fuel. Between meals, insulin falls, glucagon rises and the liver releases glucose from glycogen and then makes new glucose. In long fasts, fat breakdown provides fatty acids and ketone bodies so that the body spares protein and the brain can use alternative fuel.
deeper.intermediate: Use a diagram with four organs and arrows for each state. Include regulation: insulin activates glycogen synthase and inhibits gluconeogenic enzymes via covalent modification and gene expression; glucagon acts through cAMP and PKA. Apply to cases: in type 1 diabetes, absent insulin leads to unrestrained lipolysis and ketogenesis; in type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency lead to hyperglycaemia with usually less severe ketosis.
deeper.advanced: Integrate substrate cycling, allosteric control (for example fructose-2,6-bisphosphate) and tissue-specific isoforms (hexokinase vs glucokinase, GLUT isoforms). Consider mechanisms of insulin resistance involving lipid intermediates and inflammation, the role of the pancreatic beta cell, and drug targets such as metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists and insulin analogues. In an exam, move from molecule to patient: state the pathway change, the tissue and the physiological outcome.

commonMistakes: Treating tissues as if all had the same enzymes (liver vs muscle glycogen, for example)
Forgetting that the brain normally depends on glucose and only adapts to ketone bodies gradually
Confusing type 1 and type 2 diabetes mechanisms
Stating that fatty acids can be converted to glucose in humans

options: Muscle glycogen releasing glucose directly into blood
selfCheck.explanation: The liver releases glucose from glycogen first, then begins gluconeogenesis; muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and cannot export glucose.

selfCheck.question: Which is typical of type 2 diabetes?
options: Complete absence of insulin from birth
Insulin resistance with inadequate compensation by beta cells
Autoimmune destruction of all beta cells only
Excess insulin secretion with low glucose
selfCheck.explanation: Type 2 diabetes involves reduced insulin responsiveness and insufficient insulin secretion to overcome it.

options: Fat to be converted into glucose
The brain to use a fuel other than glucose, reducing protein breakdown
selfCheck.explanation: Ketones derived from fatty acids provide fuel for the brain and reduce the need for gluconeogenesis from muscle protein.

units.title: Regulation and Signalling: Operons, Receptors and Cascades
units.hook: Cells are not bags of enzymes running at fixed speed; they sense, decide and adjust. From the lac operon in a bacterium to insulin receptors in a human, the logic is the same: detect a signal, change an activity, produce a response and switch off again.
learningObjectives: Explain regulation of the lac operon by lactose and glucose
Describe the main classes of receptors and how they transmit signals
Explain second messengers and phosphorylation cascades
Describe how signals are terminated and amplified
Relate gene regulation to signalling and to development
Predict the effect of mutations in a signalling component

keyConcepts.definition: A prokaryotic cluster of genes under one promoter and regulated together.
A repressor binds DNA to block transcription; an inducer binds the repressor and releases it.
When glucose is available, low cAMP means CAP is inactive and lac genes are expressed poorly even if lactose is present.
A receptor that activates heterotrimeric G proteins and downstream effectors such as adenylyl cyclase.
A receptor that dimerises and autophosphorylates upon ligand binding, recruiting signalling proteins.
A small molecule such as cAMP, Ca2+ or IP3/DAG that spreads the signal inside the cell.
A series of phosphorylation steps (for example MAP kinase) that amplifies and modulates a signal.
Phosphatases, GTPase activity, receptor internalisation and second-messenger breakdown switch signals off.

deeper.beginner: The lac operon turns on only when lactose is present and glucose is low. Signalling in eukaryotes uses receptors at the cell surface that switch on internal messengers. Each step can amplify the signal, and each can be switched off.
deeper.intermediate: Compare logic: lac operon is a transcriptional switch with two inputs (inducer and cAMP-CAP); GPCR signalling uses G proteins, cAMP and PKA; RTK signalling uses Ras and kinase cascades. Predict the effect of mutations: a repressor that cannot bind the inducer gives constitutive repression; a G protein unable to hydrolyse GTP gives constitutive activation. Draw both systems side by side.
deeper.advanced: Consider network features: feedback, crosstalk, thresholds and ultrasensitivity, scaffold proteins and spatial organisation. Understand how oncogenic mutations or toxins (for example cholera toxin altering Gs) change signalling, and how drugs target kinases, receptors or second-messenger enzymes. Link signalling to gene expression via transcription factor activation.

commonMistakes: Believing that a repressor mutant that cannot bind DNA gives a repressed operon
Forgetting catabolite repression in the lac operon
Assuming all receptors work through G proteins
Overlooking signal termination

units.title: The Cell Cycle, Cancer and Disease Mechanisms
units.hook: Cancer is not one disease but a recurring set of failures in control: growth signals that never switch off, brakes that stop working and a repair system that has lost track. Seen this way, the whole of cell biology becomes a diagnostic tool.
learningObjectives: Describe the cell cycle and its checkpoints with cyclins and CDKs
Distinguish oncogenes from tumour-suppressor genes with examples
Explain the role of p53 and Rb in cell-cycle control
Relate DNA damage and repair to mutation and cancer
Use the hallmarks of cancer to organise explanations
Evaluate the principle behind targeted therapies

keyConcepts.definition: G1, S, G2 and M phases, with checkpoints that ensure DNA is intact and replicated before division.
Cyclin-dependent kinases are activated by cyclins to drive progression through the cycle.
A gain-of-function version of a growth-promoting gene (for example mutant RAS).
A gene whose loss of function promotes cancer (for example TP53, RB1).
Both alleles of a tumour-suppressor gene generally need to be inactivated for cancer to develop; one may be inherited.
A transcription factor activated by DNA damage that causes cell-cycle arrest, repair or apoptosis.
A framework of acquired capabilities such as sustained proliferative signalling, evasion of growth suppressors and resisting cell death.
A drug designed against a molecular defect in the tumour, such as a kinase inhibitor.

deeper.beginner: Normal cells divide only when told to, and check their DNA before they do. Cancer cells acquire changes that push the accelerator (oncogenes) and cut the brakes (tumour suppressors). Several changes accumulate over time.
deeper.intermediate: Use examples: a hyperactive RAS keeps growth signalling on; loss of p53 allows damaged cells to proceed; Rb normally restrains the G1/S transition. Link to DNA repair: defects in mismatch repair or BRCA genes increase mutation rate. Then use the hallmarks as a checklist to explain how a given tumour might grow, evade death and spread.
deeper.advanced: Think about evolution within a tumour: heterogeneity, selection and resistance to drugs. Consider epigenetic and metabolic changes, the microenvironment and immune evasion. Evaluate therapies by mechanism and biomarker: kinase inhibitors against BCR-ABL, receptor-targeting antibodies, PARP inhibitors exploiting synthetic lethality in BRCA-deficient cells and checkpoint inhibitors. Be clear about what each approach assumes.

commonMistakes: Saying all cancers are caused by a single gene
Treating p53 as only a gene that is 'bad' rather than a guardian of the genome
Confusing oncogene (dominant, gain of function) with tumour suppressor (recessive, loss of function)
Assuming mutation alone explains all aspects of cancer

papers.whyItMatters: An updated map of the capabilities tumours acquire, from sustained growth signalling to evading immunity. A good scaffold for organising any cancer question in an exam.

resources.title: The Cell: A Molecular Approach (2nd ed.)
resources.note: A readable free text that is good for signalling, the cell cycle and cancer.

resources.title: Molecular Biology of the Cell (4th ed.)
resources.note: A full free textbook of cell and molecular biology to revise any topic in depth.

selfCheck.question: Which statement best describes an oncogene?
options: A loss-of-function mutation in a growth-restraining gene
A gain-of-function version of a gene that promotes proliferation
A gene that only exists in viruses
selfCheck.explanation: Oncogenes are activated forms of normal proto-oncogenes, typically acting dominantly.

selfCheck.question: What is a main role of p53 after DNA damage?
options: To trigger arrest, repair or apoptosis
selfCheck.explanation: p53 acts as a transcription factor that controls responses to damage.

selfCheck.question: A person inherits one defective copy of a tumour-suppressor gene. Why does cancer risk rise?
options: The gene turns into an oncogene
Only one further hit is needed to lose both functional copies in a cell
The defective copy is dominant negative always
It increases the mutation rate of every gene by itself
selfCheck.explanation: The inherited defect is the first hit; a second somatic event removes the remaining good copy.

units.title: Techniques and Data Interpretation
units.hook: Examiners love a figure you have not seen. A gel with an odd band, a growth curve that plateaus early, a Western blot with a missing control. The skill is to ask what technique produced it, what it can measure and what it cannot.
learningObjectives: Explain the principles of PCR, electrophoresis, blotting, cloning, sequencing and CRISPR editing
Choose a technique for a given question and justify the controls
Interpret gel, blot, graph and table data
Identify artefacts and limitations of common methods
Link results to hypotheses and propose follow-up experiments
Relate techniques across courses (molecular biology, protein biochemistry, genomics)

keyConcepts.definition: Repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension with a heat-stable DNA polymerase to amplify a defined DNA segment.
Separates molecules by size (and charge) in an electric field; compare with markers.
Detects a specific protein on a membrane using an antibody after gel separation; needs a loading control.
Cutting and joining DNA fragments, for example in plasmids, to express or study genes.
An RNA-guided nuclease that cuts DNA at a chosen site, used for genome editing.
A protein expected to be constant (for example a housekeeping protein) used to check equal sample loading.
How well a method detects only the intended target and how low a level it can detect.
A signal produced by the method rather than the biology.

deeper.beginner: For each technique, ask: what is separated or amplified, how is it detected and what would a control look like? In PCR, the product size reveals the amplified region, and a no-template control checks contamination. In a Western blot, equal loading is checked with a loading control. Always check labelled axes and units on graphs.
deeper.intermediate: Practise reading data: if a band is absent in one lane, consider no protein, no loading, failed transfer or antibody problem, and use the controls to decide. For a growth curve, identify lag, log and stationary phases. For a dose-response, estimate EC50 or IC50 and ask whether replicates and error bars are shown. Propose a next experiment that distinguishes the competing explanations.
deeper.advanced: Understand limitations: PCR bias and contamination, antibody specificity, off-target CRISPR cuts and the difference between knock-out and knock-down. Consider quantitative PCR normalisation, statistical analysis and the choice between in vitro and in vivo systems. Design a decisive experiment: for example, rescue by re-expressing the gene to show that a phenotype is caused by the loss of that gene.

commonMistakes: Interpreting a missing band as proof that the protein is absent without controls
Forgetting a no-template control in PCR
Reading logarithmic axes as linear
Assuming CRISPR edits only the intended site

papers.title: A Programmable Dual-RNA-Guided DNA Endonuclease in Adaptive Bacterial Immunity
papers.authors: Jinek M, Chylinski K, Fonfara I et al
papers.whyItMatters: The in vitro study showing that Cas9, guided by an RNA, cuts DNA at a chosen site, and that the guide can be simplified to a single RNA. It is the origin of CRISPR genome editing and a model of mechanism-driven biochemistry.

papers.title: The new frontier of genome engineering with CRISPR-Cas9
papers.whyItMatters: A review by two of the discoverers on how CRISPR-Cas9 works and what it can be used for. It is a good place to connect the mechanism to applications and ethical questions.

selfCheck.question: A PCR gives a band in the sample lane and also in the no-template control. What does this suggest?
selfCheck.explanation: A band without template means something amplifiable got into the reaction.

selfCheck.question: Why use a loading control in a Western blot?
options: To check that equal amounts of protein were loaded and transferred
To reduce the size of the gel
selfCheck.explanation: Differences in band intensity are only interpretable if loading is equal.

selfCheck.question: What does the guide RNA do in CRISPR-Cas9?
options: It directs Cas9 to a matching DNA sequence
selfCheck.explanation: The guide RNA base-pairs with the target DNA and positions Cas9 to cut it.

units.title: Evaluating Evidence, and Biochemistry in Society
units.hook: The final skill is judgement. Is this claim supported? Is this therapy ready? Should we edit this gene? Answers rarely sit in a single chapter, so you draw on evidence, mechanism and ethics together and say clearly where they stop.
learningObjectives: Evaluate a scientific claim by examining design, controls, statistics and consistency
Explain reasons for irreproducibility and how good practice addresses them
Discuss ethical, legal and social issues of genetic technologies
Compare risks and benefits using evidence
Communicate a balanced position in a structured essay
Reflect on your own learning across the degree

keyConcepts.definition: The ability to obtain consistent results using the same data or methods; a cornerstone of trust.
Systematic error from design, selection, measurement or reporting.
Association does not by itself show that one factor causes another.
Research with legitimate benefits that could also be misused.
Germline changes can be inherited; somatic changes affect only the treated individual.
Caution when potential harm is serious and evidence is uncertain.
Respect for participants and fair access to benefits of research.

deeper.beginner: Ask of any claim: what was measured, compared with what, how many samples, and could chance or bias explain it? For questions about technology and society, list benefits, harms and who is affected, then give your own conclusion with reasons.
deeper.intermediate: Use a framework: scientific validity, benefit and risk, consent and fairness. For gene editing, distinguish treating somatic disease in consenting patients from heritable changes, and discuss safety, off-target effects, access and governance. Support your position with specific facts and acknowledge opposing arguments.
deeper.advanced: Engage with current issues: reproducibility in preclinical research, open data and preregistration, genomic data privacy and sharing in low- and middle-income countries, and regulation of new biotechnologies. Evaluate how scientific uncertainty should shape policy and how to communicate it to the public without exaggeration or false balance.

commonMistakes: Giving a one-sided essay on an ethical issue
Citing a single study as settled fact
Confusing what is technically possible with what is ethically acceptable
Ignoring who bears the risks and who gets the benefits

papers.title: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
papers.whyItMatters: A provocative argument that small studies, flexible analyses and a bias to publish positive results make many 'significant' findings unreliable. Whether or not you accept the strong claim, it gives you a checklist of reasons to doubt a result.

papers.title: 1,500 scientists lift the lid on reproducibility
papers.whyItMatters: A survey report showing that most researchers have failed to reproduce someone else's experiment, and many have failed to reproduce their own. It makes the case for careful records better than any lecture.

selfCheck.question: Why is correlation insufficient to show causation?
options: A third factor or reverse causation could explain the association
selfCheck.explanation: Confounding and reverse causation can produce associations without a direct causal link.

selfCheck.question: What distinguishes germline from somatic gene editing?
options: Germline edits can be inherited by future generations
selfCheck.explanation: Germline editing alters cells that pass changes to offspring, which raises additional ethical concerns.

selfCheck.question: A well-structured balanced essay on a controversial technology should:
options: Present evidence and arguments from several perspectives before reaching a justified conclusion
selfCheck.explanation: Balanced evaluation shows understanding of the issue and defends a position with reasons.
